claims.quote: The attic smelled of salt and new paint, a dry clean edge to the dust that made me cough when I tugged at the canvas.

Inside, cedar shavings smelled faintly of the same old varnish the house kept; a battered porcelain doll lay cushioned on a folded scrap of dress, its eyes sewn and its smile stitched with someone too steady to be kind.

The diary was no surprise when it turned up — a small leather thing wedged between a shoebox and a stack of knitting patterns.
A child’s hand had written, across a space like a breath: "Hush, the sea will sing you home."
claims.value: Hush, the sea will sing you home.

claims.quote: It had been shoved into a boarded alcove and covered with canvas, a blank wrapped in its own history; even under the cloth the gilt frame ridged the air with expectation.
The glass had that faint waviness older mirrors develop and a salt bloom at one edge, as if the sea had pressed the whole thing with its thumb.
When I stepped in front of it my reflection lagged by a breath and, for a second, a child's small hand pressed out from behind the glass as if from the other side.
I told myself it was the glass — the waviness, a delayed catch of light — or the draft through the boards playing tricks, or that the doll behind me might have moved in the same slatted beam of sun.
The attic was cold; my breath made a pale thread.
The yellowing sticker along its lid read, exactly, May Harper — attic inventory — 1939.
In one small cedar parcel, stitched into the lining, a folded scrap of paper had been tamped like a secret. In Aunt May’s cramped capitals it read: sewn into coat.

promises.promise: The mirror's delayed reflection and the sighting of a child's hand suggest an unresolved phenomenon the story will explore; the reader is owed an explanation or further encounter.
